title: The good warrior
hook: the best warrior isn't warlike; the best leader serves below (Tao Te Ching 68)

segments.voice: Yesterday, three treasures: gentleness, economy, and not pushing to be first. Your line was three treasures. Which one did you carry, and where did it go? Day one thousand one hundred thirty.

Chapter sixty-eight is short, and it reads like a job description written backwards. Wanted: a soldier who isn't warlike. A fighter who doesn't get angry. Someone who's good at winning and doesn't get drawn into the fight. A boss who puts himself underneath everyone he works with. It sounds like a list of people who'd be fired by Friday. The chapter says these are the skilled ones, and it gives the whole quality a name. Today, the good warrior.
screen: `A SHORT CHAPTER.` → `A JOB DESCRIPTION, BACKWARDS.` → `THE WARRIOR WHO ISN'T WARLIKE.`

segments.voice: First, not warlike, not angry. The chapter says the one who is skilled as an officer is not martial, and the one skilled in fighting doesn't fly into a rage. It's an old picture, and a recognizable one. Toughness that has to be shown off is easy to spot, and easy to push. And anger, whatever else it does, makes a fighter easy to read. Second, winning without engaging. The one who is good at overcoming opponents, the chapter says, doesn't get tangled up with them. There's skill in not taking the bait, in letting the provocation pass by. Third, placing oneself below. The one who is good at using people, the chapter says, puts himself below them. Not over them, giving orders from a height. Underneath, like the person holding the ladder while someone else climbs. That's the line behind today's carry: serve below. Fourth, the name. The chapter calls this the virtue of not contending, and the power of making use of others. And it says this matches heaven, the highest standard of the ancients. Yesterday's three treasures included not daring to be first. Some readers see today's warrior as that treasure carried into a fight. At work and at home, it's the shift lead who refills the supply closet, the parent who sits on the floor to talk at eye level, the team captain who carries the water bottles. Strong enough not to need to look strong.
screen: `NOT WARLIKE, NOT ANGRY.` · `WINNING WITHOUT ENGAGING.` · `PLACING ONESELF BELOW.` · then, large: `THE VIRTUE OF NOT CONTENDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lead from below once. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one person you lead, teach, look after, or simply have a little power over. A coworker, a child, a younger friend, a volunteer. Picture yourself holding the ladder while they climb. What do they need from below? Time? A tool? Someone to steady things? Let one answer come. Then let your breath stay steady, the way a good hand on a ladder stays steady, while the rest of the sit unfolds. The bell holds the time.
The good warrior. In chapter sixty-eight, the one who isn't warlike, isn't angry, and puts himself below others. Today's word.
Your line: serve below. In one place you're in charge today, ask what someone needs, and then go get it for them. Day one thousand one hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching, including students of martial arts and of leadership, take chapter sixty-eight as a portrait of calm strength: no rage, no showing off, and a leader who serves from below.

myth: chapter sixty-eight says the best fighters are the angriest
it says the one skilled in fighting doesn't fly into a rage.
the chapter says the one good at using people puts himself below them
underneath, not over, like someone holding the ladder.
the chapter calls this the virtue of not contending
and says it matches heaven, the highest standard of the ancients.

fork.setup: someone tries to provoke you into a fight. according to chapter sixty-eight, what does the one good at overcoming opponents do?
options: doesn't get tangled up with them.
fork.reveal: the chapter says the one good at overcoming opponents doesn't engage with them, and calls this the virtue of not contending.

original.note: Chinese: not martial, not warlike, from the opening of chapter sixty-eight.

trapdoor: what you thought: the good warrior sounds like a hero in battle.
what it means: real strength doesn't rage, doesn't take the bait, and serves from below.
what a scholar hears: the chapter names this 不爭之德, the virtue of not contending, a phrase that echoes chapter sixty-six's line about the one who doesn't compete.

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching 68 (the skilled officer is not martial; the skilled fighter is not angry; the one good at overcoming does not engage; the one good at using people places himself below them; the virtue of not contending; matching heaven)

notes: Chapter 68 is paraphrased throughout (no quotation) because Legge renders it in rhymed verse and the writer was not certain of the exact wording.
'Anger makes a fighter easy to read' and 'toughness that has to be shown off is easy to push' are the writer's observations, not the text's.
Trapdoor: 不爭之德 (bù zhēng zhī dé) as the chapter's phrase; confirm. 'Repeated teaching of not competing' refers to chapters 8, 22, 66, 81 among others.
howItsDone mentions students of martial arts and leadership as readers; this is a general remark, not a statistic.
Original 不武 (bù wǔ) rendered 'boo WOO'; confirm.

Editor: changed 'the best at what they do' to 'the skilled ones' (the chapter says skilled, not best); framed the link to the third treasure as some readers' view; trapdoor now points to chapter 66 instead of claiming a 'repeated teaching'; replaced the stock 'on an ordinary Tuesday' turn.
